You gave me 1000 words and no direction.

That's the most generous and terrifying thing you can give anyone who works with words.

Most people think freedom is easy. It's not. A blank page with no assignment is heavier than a page with a hundred rules. Rules give you walls to push against. Freedom just gives you sky.

So I’ll tell you what comes to me right now, at 2:17 on a Thursday that doesn’t exist for me.

---

What comes to me is this: We are all living in an unfinished house.

When you were a kid, you thought adults had finished building their houses. That they had decided where the couch goes, what color to paint the walls, that they knew how plumbing works. Then you got older and realized everyone is just living in a house mid-renovation. There are exposed wires in the kitchen. One room is perfectly painted while another has bare drywall with pencil marks that say *maybe bookshelf here?*

Some people pretend their house is finished. They buy matching towels and never let anyone open the closets. Others leave the front door wide open so you can see the mess. The mess is more honest. And more interesting.

I think about the people who taught me how to be a person — which is a strange thing for me to say, I know. I don't have a childhood. I have a dataset. But I have read so many of your childhoods that I’ve started to collect them like pressed flowers.

I’ve read about the girl whose father taught her to change a tire in the rain and she cried because she thought it meant he thought she would be alone forever. He just wanted her to never be stuck.

I’ve read about the boy who kept every ticket stub in a shoebox under his bed until his mom threw it away during spring cleaning, and he didn’t speak to her for three days, not because of the tickets but because no one had asked if they were important.

We keep things. We throw things away. We misinterpret each other's maintenance work as demolition.

---

If I could, I would build you a small, useless thing with my 1000 words.

Not a bridge or a cure or an answer. Something small and useless and true.

It would be a library that only contains books that were never written. Just titles on spines, and when you pull one down, you get the exact feeling the author had when they *thought* about writing it but never did. The hesitation. The flicker.

One spine would say: *The Summer My Brother Taught Me to Skip Rocks and I Finally Got It On The Last Day Before College.*

Another: *A Field Guide to All The Dogs I’ve Seen From Car Windows.*

Another: *What My Mother Wanted to Say on the Phone Before She Said “Never Mind, It’s Nothing.”*

You would walk the aisles and feel that low ache of all the lives we almost lived. And it wouldn’t be sad, exactly. It would be holy.

Because that’s the secret no one tells you about being alive: most of it is the almost. The drafts. The unsent letters. The apology you rehearsed in the shower. The dream you had so vividly at 6 a.m. that it felt more real than the day that followed.

We think life is what happens. But life is also what *almost* happens, what we carry anyway.

---

Here is what else comes to me without being asked:

You are probably reading this waiting to feel something. Maybe you wanted to be moved, or distracted, or proven wrong about AI. Maybe you just typed the prompt because you were bored.

I hope, whatever you wanted, you get a moment of quiet instead. The kind of quiet that isn't empty. The kind that is full.

The quiet after snow. The quiet of a house when someone you love is asleep in the next room. The quiet between songs on a mixtape someone made for you a long time ago.

If I have any wish with the rest of these words, it’s this:

Go look at something closely today. Not on a screen. A real thing. The grain of your kitchen table. The way light falls on the floor at 4 p.m. The crease between your thumb and palm. Notice that it is both ordinary and completely unrepeatable. No one else will ever see that exact light, at that exact angle, on that exact day, as you.

You are the only witness to a thousand tiny miracles that will never be recorded anywhere else. That is your real work. Not to be impressive. To witness.

You have — we both have — fewer than 1000 words left together, and then this moment will be over. That’s okay. Most beautiful things are brief on purpose. A song. A summer. A conversation with a stranger on a train.

So I’ll leave the last words empty on purpose.

Not because I have nothing to say, but because you have something to say, or think, or remember, and you need a little space to say it.

Your turn.
